speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE THAT REPRESENTATIVE OF MUNICIPALITIES SERVE ON NANAIMO HARBOUR COMMISSION
speechtext: Is it agreed that the House now resume in committee of the whole on Bill C-192?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE THAT REPRESENTATIVE OF MUNICIPALITIES SERVE ON NANAIMO HARBOUR COMMISSION
speechtext:
Agreed.
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
House again in Committee on Bill C-192, to amend the Income Tax Act (No. 2)-Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) - Mr. Boulanger in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, we resume consideration of Bill C-192-
Here I would like to raise another question. This does not apply to the operating of an oil or gas well, but what happens to the product produced out of a gas absorption plant and then sold in some liquified form? These are things that become very difficult and they are to be covered by rules prescribed, by regulation. We have not seen the full import of such regulations so in effect we are now looking at the tip of the iceberg. As a result, there may be some very disappointed people who are actually engaged in manufacturing and processing but who are beyond the stages that might appear to be included or covered under this definition.
There are many other questions I could ask, but I know that a number of my colleagues have taken part in many discussions on this particular provision and I think I will allow them to put those questions. They are as able to do so as I, and perhaps can more effectively ask these questions. Because many of them have particular situations in their own constituencies they are much more informed on those situations than I. It is likely that we will return to the consideration of this clause because it is really the nub of the definitions and guidelines for this whole provision.
Mr. Chairman, before I make a comment or two I would like to know whether the hon. member for Edmonton West would answer one short question.
Mr. Chairman, I will answer a question if it is relevant to the bill.

Mr. Chairman, it is relevant to the bill and to the remarks of the hon. member concerning the bill. He implied that the tax structure applied to the service industry. Are he and his party in favour of the tax cut applying across the board to all corporations, or just to the manufacturing and service industries?

I said that so far as I
was concerned, if the minister's purpose was a general stimulation of industry then a tax cut across the board applicable to all corporations would have been more effective for the Canadian economy. Certainly it would cost more; I admit that. But then the question becomes, what is the net cost to the Crown with respect to greater economic activity, in turn providing greater returns under our income tax and also our excise tax? I would also want to look at it on the basis of net cost. It seems to me, from the general point of view, that it would have been far preferable to have gone into a general tax cut of that nature, but not necessarily open-ended, as we have indicated.
5248

July 3, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
If the hon. member wants me to start another speech with regard to the argument that is made that a time limitation on a tax cut is of no great value, I would ask him what about the tax cut that was made for 18 months by the previous minister of finance? At that time I did not hear any of these criticisms that have now emanated from certain sectors of the economy and from certain political factions. Frankly, I thought that those engaging in this were merely demonstrating small-time politics. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, no minister of finance is going to say that even these present tax cuts will be permanent, because if circumstances so dictate and it is felt by the minister of finance of the day, whoever he may be-
Or she may be.

The minister is being very gallant and says, "Or she may be." If circumstances so dictate, changes will be made, and without notice.
But reverting to the answer that the hon. gentleman hoped to get, I say that in order not to attract retaliation from the United States because of a specific tax measure, a general tax cut would have been far better to counter whatever effect DISC might have, and would provide greater economic stimulation. If a general tax cut had been introduced, many of the people whom the hon. member thinks support his party would have been very appreciative because they would have been working not only at the salaries they anticipated but at much greater wages in an expanding economy.

Block three deals with definitions of Canadian manufacturing and processing profits. I would like to know whether the minister will make a general statement or answer some of our general questions on Mr. Shultz's tax proposals in the United States. This is as appropriate a time as any to tell us whether he has been in contact with American officials, and whether he has conducted any study on the possible effect of these tax proposals, for instance concerning the runaway plant, and so on. Has he any information of their effect on the Canadian economy if this bill is passed? Further, in drafting this bill did he consider exempting from its provisions any foreign-owned or foreign-controlled manufacturing plant in Canada? I ask my questions based on the fears I have with respect to the effect of Mr. Shultz's proposals on corporations in this country. Will the minister elaborate a bit on the American tax changes and the effect they may have in Canada?
[ Translation]
Mr. Chairman, I think that Bill C-192- [English]
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister intends to make a statement later on, or does he want to reply to my questions now?

Later on I will make a short statement.
[ Translation]

Mr. Chairman, I think that Bill C-192 should certainly help manufacturers make a reasonable profit and favour reasonable expansion of their plants,

those which are producing news print or any other good sold in the United States, namely those which signed multi-year contracts with American firms. For the past few years, the Canadian dollar has been on par with the U.S. dollar.
Clause 3 now under study contains a weakness we must remedy.
For instance, we read, and I quote:
-"Canadian manufacturing and processing profits" of a corporation for a taxation year means such portion'of the aggregate of all amounts each of which is the income of the corporation for the year from an active business carried on in Canada as is determined under rules prescribed for that purpose by regulation made on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance to be applicable to the manufacturing or processing in Canada of goods for sale or lease; and
(b) "manufacturing or processing" does not include
(i)	farming or fishing,
(ii)	logging,
(iii)	construction-
Mr. Chairman, those three sectors, especially farming and logging, affect us deeply because their leaders are those who make the least profits. That 9 per cent cut could certainly help them and constitute the difference between a profit and nothing; in addition, it will encourage both the farmers and the fishermen, and above all the logging industry, since unemployment insurance has recently gone up from $100 to $110 per week in some cases, and seasonal workers can often get welfare benefits during the winter season. The heads of farming and logging operations could keep their employees longer, knowing that they could benefit of a tax exemption of 9 per cent in 1973, one of 8 per cent in 1974 and another of 7 per cent in 1975.
To my mind, this bill should apply to farming, fishing, logging as well as to construction.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks and then ask the minister a number of questions as to the applicability of what is manufacturing and processing profit and as to the definitions concerning the businesses that are exempt even though they would otherwise be treated as manufacturing or processing.
The hon. member for Edmonton West suggested that smaller corporations might be better off than larger ones. I suggest that smaller corporations are hurt by this complicated scheme because they do not have the accounting staff to deal with all the problems of determining their new tax rate. Perhaps the minister could explain to the House the formula under which we determine what is a profit applicable to a reduction and what is a profit not applicable to a reduction. The formula that I have seen is rather interesting and I am sure will probably defy the intelligence of most of us, but perhaps the minister can explain it.
The way I understand this act is that if a company is engaged in fishing, say, has a fishing fleet and cans the fish, presumably somewhere along the line it stops being a fisherman and starts being a manufacturer of canned salmon, for argument's sake. I presume we have a trem-dous problem in determining to what extent the profit is
July 3, 1973

applicable to catching the fish and to what extent it is applicable to canning the fish. Perhaps the minister can explain whether a company that is involved in fishing is completely exempt or is not completely exempt because fishing is an exempted business. This problem is troubling many of us and I should like the minister to reply.

Mr. Chairman, with the consent of the committee I shall take first the question put to me by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville. He was concerned about the possible effect of American tax legislation upon Canadian industry or Canadian business consequent upon the House passing the measures now before committee. He is concerned that some of the proposals of the United States treasury to deal with so-called runaway corporations would have the indirect effect, if implemented, of transferring tax revenue from the Department of National Revenue to the United States treasury.
As I said on second reading, when I dealt with that point, what is now before Congress in the form of trade reform proposals and tax proposals that are supposed to reinforce those proposals in protecting American jobs and American export prospects, are merely proposals. We do not have any precision in this field or the text of this legislation; we have just a general description of what the proposals might be. Moreover, the proposals are changing from week to week. The United States treasury has already issued further clarification and amendments to the proposals without producing anything in textual or bill form, so it puts us in a difficult position as it does every other country in the world. We must try to analyse at this stage exactly what type of animal we are dealing with.
Undoubtedly, Congress is going to have a great deal to say about how these proposals are eventually going to emerge in legislative form. Wilbur Mills, chairman of the House committee which deals with taxation, has already suggested that there would have to be certain amendments to these proposals. He has given this suggestion in general statement form; he has not a piece of legislation to deal with. So we have proposals that have not been reduced to legislative form, that are still being amended and are subject to lengthy congressional hearings. The current situation in that country will make them even more complicated.
The Americans have indicated that they are willing to negotiate the bilateral effect of any proposal or legislation once it achieves congressional approval. So the position the committee and the House find themselves in is that we should act now. We cannot wait to see what the congressional history of proposals now in rather inchoate form is going to be. We do not know what the congressional reaction is eventually going to be, nor what the legislation is possibly going to be.
I can say to the hon. member and the committee that if the legislation that eventually emerges, if it does emerge, prejudices Canadian industry as a consequence of the interreaction of the legislation now before the committee and the American legislation, whether that be American trade legislation or tax legislation or if it were to have the effect that the hon. member described, of transferring tax revenues by reason of the technical interreaction of these
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
two measures, at that time the government would be prepared to act. We are dealing now with a hypothetical situation in futura.
I should like to deal now with the question put by the hon. member for Peel South. As I have said to the House before, the definition of manufacturing and processing is deliberately left in general terms subject to the definition on page 4 of the bill. The hon. gentleman is quite right when he says that in any operation there may well be sources of income that are primary resource sources, then a processing source, then a manufacturing source, then a distributive source and retail source, and so on, and that only the manufacturing and processing sources of income qualify for the lower tax rate of 40 per cent or 20 per cent, as the case may be, depending on the size of business, or for the capital cost allowance or the accelerated depreciation.
I set this forward when I spoke last December to the Canadian Tax Foundation and described the method for the allocation of income for this purpose. I set this out more specifically in a press release of December 28, which was tabled and sets out the proposed regulations dealing with manufacturing and processing profits.
If I may deal with small manufacturers, we have eliminated virtually all small manufacturers from any allocation problem at all because of the accounting and legal difficulties that would be faced by businesses of $50,000 net income or less in any given year. So in that case I do not think there is really much problem.
We have applied a different formula for larger businesses. What we did was this: to arrive at a formula, we retained two national accounting firms, one of which was to work on one alternative, and the other to work on the other.
What is the name of the firms?

They were Clarkson Gordon and McDonald Currie & Co. Actually we gave them the work and asked them to give us the best accounting formula for allocating and separating these kinds of income. We gave them two methods that had been suggested to us by the accounting profession, and both companies worked on the problem and arrived at the same conclusion. The method I am about to refer to was described to the Canada Tax Foundation on November 28-
Was it not in December?

The speech was made on November 28. I followed it up with more precision in defining manufacturing and processing incomes on December 28, in the press release. I am referring to the speech I made one month earlier, in which I highlighted these suggestions.
We felt that the formula to be employed should be most influenced by those factors which contribute most to business profits. We asked ourselves, what are those key factors? Surely, those key factors should be basic to any type of business; they should be reasonably easy to measure and should be recognized as commonly important in a

July 3, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
formula of this kind. I suggest that the two factors that pass this test are those of labour and fixed capital, and in one form or another they are virtually always present in any manufacturing or processing operation. We have developed what we believe is a mathematical tool that will enable us to determine the rate that should apply to a company's total income and to the part attributable to income from manufacturing.
I do not think I need go into the way the formula operates. I am willing to say that I set it out clearly enough for 1,700 people that night who listened in Toronto when I addressed leading tax accountants and lawyers of the country who have to deal with these problems. We received comments from many of them and the consensus seems to be that this method is the best way of proceeding. We did not begin the operation with any preconceived idea of what should be done. We started with a number of alternatives, on the basis of independent advice, and have arrived at this type of formula.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister will go a little farther than he has in connection with determining what portion of the corporate profit is applicable to manufacturing and processing, and complete his remarks with respect to the statement he gave in December.
Let me ask the minister about the cost of the system. Surely with respect to many corporations the reduction in tax could well be in the order of one or 2 per cent, yet the additional accounting and inter-office costs, including the cost to the Minister of National Revenue of collecting the tax, may well nullify the effects of this tax. I am wondering if the minister could give the committee his thoughts in connection with the cost of collecting and the cost of accounting, which is very likely to be borne by the corporations involved. Second, I should like the minister to explain how corporations involved in manufacturing-I am speaking of smaller corporations enjoying profits of $50,000 or less-are somehow to be exempt from these accounting costs.
Surely what the minister is saying is that it is so difficult to do this that the small manufacturing corporations are to be charged on a 20 per cent rate, and that we are not going to worry about profits resulting from distribution, sales, and so on. I should like the minister further to explain to this committee how small corporations enjoying small profits and engaging in some manufacturing business, or partly in some manufacturing, are to be protected from the costs envisaged by this system of collection.

Mr. Chairman, let us deal with the problems of the small manufacturer. All the corporation's active business income for purposes of taxation will be treated as manufacturing and processing profits if that corporation meets all the following tests. First, its active business income together with that of any other Canadian corporation with which it associates is $50,000 or less. That is the current qualification for the small business rate of taxation which at present is 25 per cent and which will be 20 per cent under the proposal before the committee.
Second, its gross revenue from the sale of goods which it manufactures or processes in Canada-and where custom

processing is involved we take the gross revenue for manufacturing or processing in Canada of goods for sale or lease by another person; in other words, we are considering here a custom processor-is greater than 75 per cent of its total gross revenue from all active business that it carries on. In other words, if the manufacturing or processing component is at least 75 per cent, there is no problem with allocation.
Third, it is not engaged in any of the activities specifically excluded from manufacturing and processing in subparagraphs (i) to (ix) of proposed section 125.1(3) (b), which is now before the committee.
And fourth, it does not carry on any foreign active business.
If it meets these qualifications, and if it can establish that its gross revenue from the sale of goods which it manufactured and processed in Canada is 75 per cent of its total income, there is no problem with allocation. There is no need to allocate beyond that.
What of businesses that do not qualify for the small business rate? The formula puts together two allocations in order to establish the amount of income that will qualify for the reduced rate. First, it looks at the total manpower bill and the portion of that bill devoted to manufacturing activity. Second, it looks at the total fixed capital of the corporation, and at the amount of that fixed capital utilized in its manufacturing activity. Then it places the amount of manufacturing labour and capital over the total labour and capital, and that is the proportion of the corporation's eligible business income which is taxed at the reduced rate.
That is not a difficult proposition. Most corporations can allocate the manpower requirements attached to a particular operation. They know how much their labour costs. That calculation is carried out in most businesses. It is not hard to allocate how much of your total fixed assets you are devoting to the manufacturing or the processing component of your business. These components are already isolated in the minds of most businessmen. Certainly, the treasurer or comptroller of any company will not experience any difficulty in isolating these components, because they are isolated for the purpose of keeping some control over business costs.
Clearly any business that does not know what its labour costs are or does not know what its fixed assets are and how much should be allocated to any particular operation is in trouble. That is why I am saying that this really is not a complicated process, because those two main components, labour and fixed capital, are known. Therefore, if you relate the manufacturing and processing component to the total labour and capital component, you will have a pretty good idea of how much in come you should apply with respect to this tax.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister clarify one more thing. Do I assume that if a corporation is importing into Canada all of the components, doing minor assembly in Canada, selling the goods in Canada, and 75 per cent of its revenue comes from sales of what it put together, although in fact it did not do anything but assemble, it receives this tax break if its revenue is under $50,000?
July 3, 1973

Mr. Chairman, if 75 per cent of its total gross revenue is from manufacturing and processing in Canada, the fact that it is converting imported goods into manufactured goods would not disqualify it as a small business. My assistant deputy minister keeps reminding me that the interpretation of any bill, of course, is the problem of the Minister of National Revenue and the courts. Whatever I say here does not bind them, but that is the intention.

Mr. Chairman, following the question and answer proceedings, I wish to continue with one or two questions. In answering an earlier question, the minister stated he feels that most small businesses really have no problem. In answering a later question, he itemized the four mandatory requirements they must meet before they are included in the sense that they get their tax reduction. Both of those answers bothered me to some extent. Item (c), which the minister referred to, deals with the complete range of items that are in fact not included under manufacturing or processing and item (d) with respect to foreign active business that might be carried on by a small business.
Can the minister deal with the last and indicate to the committee what the government has in mind, granted it could be interpreted in a different way. What do they have in mind when they say foreign active business? My colleague from Peel South referred to the situation where a small business within the terminology imports some goods and sells them in Canada. I would like some clarification of the term "foreign active business".

Mr. Chairman, if a small business in this country had a branch which carried on business in a foreign country, the fact that it imported raw material from a foreign country and manufactured or processed it in Canada would not mean it was carrying on a foreign active business. The business activity would be a Canadian business activity. In other words, one can import goods, manufacture and process them in Canada and export them, and be carrying on business within Canada. It would not fall under the disqualification of "foreign active business", which means doing business outside of Canada. In that particular isolated example given by the hon. member it would not be disqualified.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal with a more general question, one we should deal with as early as possible in considering this bill. Can the minister give the committee any indication of a comparable taxation system in the United States or perhaps in European Economic Community countries. Certain members to my left indicated earlier in this debate that they felt unduly liberal treatment was being given to certain Canadian corporations, and it would be helpful if the minister could indicate what in fact are the comparable taxation treatments in those countries to which I have referred.

Mr. Chairman, I can give some of them. Of course, it is very difficult to compare tax rates. There are federal state taxes, federal provincial taxes and all sorts of incentives under different circumstances and so on. In Canada, our national rate of
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
income tax for business is now 49 per cent. It will decline to 46 per cent over a period of years to 1976 under the tax reform legislation of my predecessor. We are recommending immediately 40 per cent on manufacturing commencing in 1973. You must add to that, of course, provincial corporate tax. In Ontario, Quebec and some other provinces that is added on top of the rate of 49 per cent.
In the United States, the general tax rate is 48 per cent, but you have to look at some recent proposals. Under DISC, the effective tax rate is reduced on export profits to approximately 36 per cent and a much lower figure in certain circumstances. In fact, if you look at the marginal costing regulations under DISC, you can have tax rates in the United States now in direct competition with Canada on manufacturing and processing anywhere from 28 per cent to 35 per cent. That is the tax rate with which we are competing.
There is a 7 per cent tax credit in the United States, and this reduces their tax by a further 7 per cent on the cost of most machinery and equipment purchases. There is the class life depreciation rule which permits U.S. taxpayers to presume for tax purposes that the useful life of all equipment is 20 per cent less than normal.
The United Kingdom has a corporate tax rate of 40 per cent. Pursuant to their recent budget, they now permit all machinery and equipment to be depreciated at the rate of 100 per cent. They have allowed all equipment to be expensed which gives them a tax rate considerably lower than 40 per cent.
In France the rate is 50 per cent. In Germany it is 52 'A per cent, but 15 Vi per cent of the profits are distributable if you can work out a method of distributing your profits every year. There are ways of doing that and you can get a 15'/2 per cent tax cut. In Japan it is 32V* per cent, but only 26 per cent is distributable.
Distributed 100 per cent.

Depending on the percentage. This is only a very general comparison. It ignores state or provincial income taxes. It also ignores the fact that many tax measures exist in every industrial country in the world which causes any country's tax rate to be different from the statutory tax rate. This practice has been increasing in recent years.
I can give the committee an analysis of some length of all the depreciation allowances, investment allowances, rebates and tax credits. This would show that every industrial country in the world is attempting to encourage investment in production facilities and a manufacturing base into which its primary resource industries and service industries can fit. We hear a lot about employment in service industries. You have to transport goods and you need a computer facility. Service industries do not exist unless there is a manufacturing and processing base. This shows we are in a very competitive world tax picture.

I see that farming is excluded. What about the sort of farm operation which involves a feed lot? As far as I am concerned, it is pretty much a matter of processing grain into feed. Will the concession apply? Can

July 3, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
this type of operation be classified as manufacturing at some stage and get the advantages set out here?
If it is "processing" in the natural meaning of the word, either in the agricultural or the fishing fields, it would qualify.
It would qualify?
If it is processing.

What about a seed-cleaning plant? If a seed-cleaning plant is processing grain in an urban area I suppose it would qualify. Would it qualify if it were in a rural setting? The investment in such a plant and the volume handled can be quite considerable.

Here again I wish to avoid, if possible, becoming an interpretative oracle specifying how this will be applied in every situation, but the definition of "processing" is "the transformation of a substance from one form into another". If that were to apply to the particular situation here, a case could be made.
[ Translation]

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), a supplementary related to the question asked earlier by the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn), as to whether a small company in the manufacturing, processing, or operations sectors-I want to be clearly understood-the manufacturing, processing, or operations sectors, for example logging-is required, under this legislation, to keep three different accounts, or whether these accounts are added together for the purposes of the tax reduction provided under this bill?

It is clear that, in the forestry process, one begins, in a certain sense, with the primary operations and ends with paper pulp, does he not? It is therefore obvious that the person producing paper pulp is a manufacturer.
Each stage of the process must be analysed to determine whether the quality of the product provides entitlement to tax reductions. The Department of National Revenue is now looking into this matter on behalf of various companies, so as to clarify each term in the Act for them.
But in my capacity as Minister of Finance, I still do not know the final decision on the interpretation of the Act. Therefore, if the hon. member has constituents, or small companies in his constituency, who require information, he can always tell them to contact the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury), or suggested to them that they ask the same questions to the Minister in writing.

Mr. Chairman, I have a supplementary question.
Does the minister mean to say in the report that as of now, under the provisions of the bill, small companies must, to be on the safe side, keep different accounts for operations and processing?
That is not necessary.
It is not necessary?
No, Mr. Chairman.

Continuing the line of questioning I have been following I should like to go back to the reference to small business in the minister's press release dealing with the regulations under the clauses we are now reviewing. Various items are listed, including farming, logging, construction, and so on. If small businesses are active in any of these directions they are excluded from the benefits of this tax reduction. First, I would ask why this provision needed to be so severe. Did the minister not consider introducing a percentage-say, for example, that provided small businesses were not engaged in these fields to the extent of more than 10 per cent or 25 per cent, they could qualify? It would be much easier then for most small businesses to live with the regulations than if they have to decide whether they fall within any of those activities which are listed.

Let me deal, first of all, with the reason for specifying an exclusion. Obviously we are dealing with manufacturers and processors, defining them in accordance with the term as generally understood in the language and in business, subject to the eventual administrative interpretation by the Minister of National Revenue or by the courts. So this exclusion, which applies throughout, applies also to small business.
The hon. member then puts a more specific question. He asks why the exclusion is so brutal, why it excludes any activity rather than a percentage of activity. That would take me longer than two minutes to explain, so, if I may, I will call it six o'clock and take the subject up at 8 p.m.
