AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.
The House resumed consideration in committee of Bill C-192, to amend the Income Tax Act (No. 2)-Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton)-Mr. Laniel in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. When the House rose at six o'clock the committee was considering subparagraph (3) of Bill C-192 which can be found at pages 3, 4 and the upper part of 5.

Mr. Chairman, I think we were talking about the question posed by the hon. member for York-Simcoe in respect of the problem of excluding the definition of manufacturing and processing found at page 4 of the bill, and then applying that to the allocation of manufacturing and processing profits, which is found in the proposed income tax regulations tabled at the request of the hon. member for Edmonton West.
The question was why in the case of a small business a corporation attempting to qualify for the low rate on processing profits should not be engaged in any of the activities specifically excluded. I suppose the first comment I should make is that the mere fact that a small manufacturing corporation cannot qualify for the special rule, that is to say, the special rule which exempts a corporation from the allocation rule, does not represent a severe penalty. It merely means that a corporation cannot automatically qualify for the reduced rate, but it can use the formula in order to benefit in relation to manufacturing and processing income. In other words, if it could allocate successfully, as most companies can, the labour content applied to manufacturing and processing, that proportion of its fixed assets allocated to manufacturing and processing, there would be no trouble.
The basic reason for the rule I think is apparent. Consider a company that is principally in the primary manufacturing business, or a primary manufacturer, which does some secondary manufacturing and processing. For example, a gravel quarry, which is primary, which does some processing of the raw gravel, and 90 per cent of the profit of this company is derived from the quarry operation and
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
10 per cent from processing. Without this rule more than 75 per cent of the company's income would fall under the term "manufacturing or processing", to use the words in the bill, but it should not be able to qualify 100 per cent of its business income as manufacturing or processing income. In other words, the amount of its activity may not reflect the amount of profit from that activity. The special rule in the bill is designed to deal with this type of situation.
I suppose the rule is arbitrary, but it must be in order to maintain simplicity. The whole purpose of the rule is to provide a simple test for the smaller corporations, and therefore any attempt we might make to be more flexible, more selective or more scientific would make the regulations more complex and, therefore, self-defeating in terms, of what we are attempting to do in the first place; that is, to make the whole matter a little more simple.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might put a further question to the Minister of Finance dealing again with his release of December 28. I would ask whether he might perhaps elaborate on the formula referred to in describing what "ML" stands for. It is pointed out that it is 100 over 75, which I understand means there is a $25 addition to the labour content of $75 in order to have a certain overhead component in the calculation.
The minister mentioned earlier that the two professional firms, Clarkson Gordon and McDonald Currie advised him. I was wondering what information they gave to justify this as being an equitable relationship between iabour content and general overhead. Would the minister agree that, because of certain of the regulations, in any event it is very unlikely such a firm would qualify for the full tax reduction suggested, in other words from 49 per cent to 40 per cent, particularly as it refers to "the lesser of"?
I am not sure what the hon. member is getting at in his argument.
The formula is simple.

I would like to take the hon. gentleman through the formula. What it says is that the manufacturer's profit for the purpose of the rate reduction is its active business income earned in Canada, other than its resource profits; then the following equation is applied to those profits: ML plus MC over TL plus TC. That means the proportion of labour costs attributable to manufacturing and processing income plus that proportion of fixed assets attributable to manufacturing and processing income over the total labour cost plus the total fixed asset cost. It is very simple, and I think I have explained the language that the hon. member wanted.
As to whether this is the best formula, we sought advice, independent of the advisers I have, from the accounting profession as to which method was the simplest, most equitable and easiest to operate, as well as least expensive in the allocation of income, and this was the advice we received. As I said earlier before the dinner break, I think that since any business that knows where it stands is able in any event to allocate its labour costs, to itemize those

July 3, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
costs against various aspects of its operation, if it can locate its percentage of fixed assets against its total process and parts of that process, and if it has any idea of where it stands in terms of cost control, this formula makes sense, because the two primary elements in the manufacturing operation are labour costs and capital.

Mr. Chairman, do I take it from the minister's comments that he is not able to offer us tonight the actual background reason that his advisers gave for the setting of those two formulae? I am referring also to the 100 over 75 reference. What I am mainly after is whether the minister could indicate if there is a range. If they are suggesting there is a $25 component for every $75 of labour, did his advisers indicate that, in the case of certain companies that may be affected by this act, the range could have been $30, $40 or $15? Was there a range or did they, quite fortunately, pick exactly the formula that was applicable to all operations?

These are arbitrary figures. One has to take decisions. We examined the problem within the Department of Finance and the problem was also examined within the Department of National Revenue. We sought advice and we evaluated it, and then we made our own decision. Certainly the reaction we have received from those cognizant of a rather technical field both in the legal and accounting professions seems to substantiate our opinion that this is a relatively fair way to assess it.

Mr. Chairman, may I put a further question to the minister. On page 4 of his release he refers to various components that will go into the total labour content of his formula, and he mentioned that it will not includes fees paid to independent salesmen. I felt it would be helpful if he could define more fully for the committee what he means by "independent salesmen". Does this simply refer to salesmen on a commission basis, or in what way did he distinguish between an independent salesman and, presumably, some other type of person when using this term?

The hon. gentleman is quoting from a press release. The wording will be more precise in the regulations. What we wanted to include were those labour costs and fixed asset costs that were directly attributable to the manufacturing or processing aspect. The indirect cost will have to be taken into account as well. An independent contractor or salesman, somebody in the distributing, retail or sales process, is of course outside that direct process, and that is why we wanted to keep it outside the direct total labour cost.

If I may start a more general line of questioning, Mr. Chairman, may I remind the minister that in committee he was questioned with respect to the percentage of businesses in Canada that he believed will have the benefit of this legislation if the bill passes. Could he tell the committee whether he has any more up to date information on the percentage of businesses in Canada that will actually feel the impact of this bill and, secondly, to what degree are they foreign controlled?

I will try to be as specific as I can. Let us look at the number of corporations that are eligible. There will be approximately 110,000 tax paying corporations in Canada, of which 100,000 will be small corporations, that is to say having a taxable income of less than $50,000. Approximately 10,000 of the small corporations will have manufacturing as their principal activity, and they should receive the 20 per cent rate on their entire taxable income. Of the remaining 90,000 small corporations, a significant number, perhaps another 5,000, will be taxed at the 20 per cent rate on a portion of their income which will depend on the extent to which they are engaged in manufacturing as against other activities.
It is very difficult to estimate the proportion of the 10,000 large corporations that will benefit from the 40 per cent tax rate. The larger corporations, as the hon. member knows, tend to be more diversified, and the number of corporations that are engaged in manufacturing and processing to any extent will appear high. The portion of the total taxable income that will benefit from the 40 per cent rate would be more meaningful. In other words, rather than take the number of corporations that may be eligible, we should try to take a look at what the total proportion of corporate income is that would be eligible.
Of the 10,000 large corporations, approximately 3,000 have manufacturing as their principal activity, and they should receive the 40 per cent rate on most of their income. Perhaps another 2,000 corporations will receive the 40 per cent rate on a portion of their income because they are engaged in the manufacturing process to a lesser degree. Approximately 5 per cent of all corporate taxable income will be taxed at the reduced 20 per cent rate and an additional 35 per cent will be taxed at the 40 per cent rate. Manufacturing represents about 40 per cent of the total corporate taxable income in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I do not want to limit the hon. member for York-Simcoe but I think that some of his colleagues have been seeking the floor and I know that the minister has put to the committee quite a lot of information. Perhaps we could give a chance to the colleagues of the hon. member and return to him in a few moments. However, at this point I will allow him an extra question.

I wonder whether the minister could answer the second part of my question which was: To what extent are the corporations to which he referred-let us take the 5,000 the 3,000 and the 2,000 large corporations-foreign controlled?
We cannot give the committee that precise information.
What about an estimate?

We will make an estimate of the figures we have. Of all the manufacturing profits in Canada, I would say approximately 60 per cent are earned by foreign controlled corporations and 40 per cent by Canadian controlled corporations. Just as significant a fact is that these foreign controlled corporations employ about one million Canadians directly and affect
July 3, 1973

the employment of another one million Canadians indirectly.

Mr. Chairman, prior to the dinner break the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar put some questions to the minister in connection with the matter of a feed lot operation, and asked him whether that feed lot operation was considered a farming operation. The minister suggested that perhaps it was processing and therefore might be excluded.
Will the minister still confirm that a feed lot is no longer termed as farming under the provisions of the Income Tax Act? Or, Mr. Chairman, is it a manufacturing operation, and will the minister suggest changes in the act? Will he clarify the situation now?

Here again, Mr. Chairman, it is a matter for interpretation of every individual business as the facts are presented to the Minister of National Revenue and, on appeal, to the courts. It may well be that some part of a feed lot operation could be processing, but without absolute precision on the factual details I would not be in a position to interpret that. Nor, frankly, is it my function to interpret, since anything I would say here would not necessarily be binding on a court of law.

If the minister is not prepared to define this bill with precision, does he expect us to go ahead with the bill? The whole question of interpretation and definition is rather essential to subclause (3) that we are discussing here.
We have had a question concerning farming. Where does farming end and begin? Where does processing end and begin? I refer to the case of a potato chip operator, making chips from potatoes, and to the case of a fishing company that goes into canning and processing and the making of fish cake.
I would like to know from the minister where logging ends and lumbering begins, the making of lumber and plywood products. In view of some of the obvious shortages of these commodities on the market, and the huge inflation rate that has developed in these commodities since May 8, 1972, would the minister at this point be prepared to remove fishing, farming, and logging in particular from the classification where activities in those fields are not treated as manufacturing and processing, so that as a result of this tax reduction we could look forward to stimulating these industries in their activities?

You know, Mr. Chairman, I stated before the Standing Committee on Finance that leaving the definition of manufacturing and processing to be general, and allowing the words to be interpreted subject to the exclusions in the bill, according to general business and accounting practices, reinforced by jurisprudence, was far more favourable to the taxpayer than an itemized list of what might or might not be manufacturing and processing, against which every legal situation would have to be judged. I suggest to the committee that the taxpayer will receive far better treatment under this general type of interpretation. There are many words in the
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
Income Tax Act that are not more precise than "manufacturing and processing." I can cite a number.
There is no definition in the Income Tax Act of "income". There is no definition in the Income Tax Act of "profit". There is no definition in the Income Tax Act of "foreign". There is no definition in the Income Tax Act of the word "control". You have to rely on the general understanding of the English language and on general business and accounting terms.
I am suggesting to the hon. member that the taxpayer generally will be better served by general definitions than by specific definitions which, by the very fact of being rendered explicit, exclude that which is not included. I am sure the hon. member for Broadview remembers that principle very well.
As to the latter part of the hon. gentleman's question, the reason that the manufacturing and processing industries, in the opinion of the government, are being given a lower tax rate is because, above all others, they are subject to direct foreign competition, and the jobs supported by those industries are subject to that type of competition. Service industries are sheltered by the very nature of those industries themselves although, as I said earlier today, they depend for their health on the manufacturing complex in this country. Primary resource industries depend on world markets and general supply and demand, but they are not subject to that particular type of competition, against which this bill is meant to fight.

Mr. Chairman, I am amazed that the minister would suggest that this legislation should not be extended to exclude farming and fishing, but going on to subparagraph (vi) I note that a company involved in processing ore to the primary metal cannot qualify for the lower tax rate. Is it the view of the minister that it is not in the interests of Canada to encourage companies to process or smelt ore to primary metal? This is the kind of manufacturing witch we on this side of the House think should be encouraged in Canada. Is it the view of the minister that a company that decides to smelt its raw ore into primary metal should not receive any tax break as a result of this particular legislation?

Of course, in the primary resource field, Mr. Chairman, we already have a number of incentives some of which do not meet with favour in certain quarters in this House. We have depletion allowances. We have accelerated depreciation. We have the expensing of exploration and development costs, and so on, for mining and the oil industries.
When we get into processing the very point of the processing incentive, in terms of accelerated depreciation and the lower tax rate, is to encourage further processing of our own primary resources in this country-metal, ore, oil and gas-by giving corporations the benefit of this 40 per cent rate. So that in Alberta and British Columbia we can encourage the petrochemical industries to refine the mineral resources of those provinces, and the same thing in northern Saskatchewan and Manitoba. This would also apply in other parts of our provinces that have natural resources.
I believe that Canadians, and quite rightly so, want to process more of those resources here, and that is the very

July 3, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
point of the processing incentive-not only manufacturing but processing. To answer the hon. member for Peel South, the manufacturing benefit is nationwide to encourage the development of a manufacturing base in the Atlantic provinces, which the Atlantic Development Council suggests is so necessary, as well as in western Canada. Even further than that, it will broaden the industrial base of the country closer to the natural resources. I am glad that the hon. gentleman is nodding his head because finally he sees the impact of this bill.

That is precisely the point. The bill excludes the activity, for a tax reduction of processing to a primary metal stage, or its equivalent of a mineral resource. That is the very point. Therefore I expect the minister, having made that glowing nationalist statement, to exclude from this particular subclause that very item. Because this bill provides that if a company engages in a smelting operation to bring ore to primary metal state, that particular activity does not qualify that company for a tax reduction. I think the minister does not understand his own bill. That is exactly what I am getting at, and I am proud that the minister finally realizes that in his statement. Will the minister remove subparagraph (vi) from subclause (3)?

Let me go at this again and just go through these words. There may be ambivalence in the word "processing" here. This bill uses the words "processing to the prime stage" in the exclusion rule. That is not the definition of processing within the ambit of the bill. Anything processed to the prime metal stage is already covered by depletion provisions, accelerated depreciation and the expensing of exploration and development costs. These incentives are already built into the primary resource process.
So what this exclusion does is to say; "We are excluding that processing up to the prime metal stage because you have already got accelerated depreciation, you have already got the depletion and you have already got the expensing." Processing is from the prime metal stage to the secondary stage. Perhaps it is the ambivalence of the word "processing" that has misled the hon. member. If that is so, I want to apologize to him.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a few questions. I was wondering what the estimated cost of these tax changes would be; secondly, what would have been the estimated cost if they were applied across the board to all corporations; thirdly, what is the estimated cost of the fast write-offs?
Would you give me the third again, please?

First, the estimated cost to the Treasury of the corporation tax cuts to manufacturing and processing; secondly, did the minister make any estimation of what would have been the total cost if it had been applied to all corporations; thirdly, what would be the fast write-offs cost to the federal Treasury?

If we are talking about 40 per cent of Canadian corporations receiving the rate which is charged, half a billion dollars, then 100 per cent represents $1,250 million. I have not got the breakdown of the capital cost allowance here but I could try to get it for the hon. gentleman. It might be a little difficult because we cannot anticipate the extent of spending intentions and what equipment is going to be purchased to take advantage of that allowance.

Before the dinner hour the minister gave quite an account of how other countries treated their corporations. I do not recall him answering whether other countries have varying rates of taxation to apply to different segments of the industry or different types of corporations as this bill proposes.
In general terms, the answer is yes, but I would have to give the hon. gentleman a book in order to break it down for him.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask if grain handling and grain transportation could be included in this. We are exporting a couple of billion dollars worth of feed and are looking at a couple of good years ahead of us, but we have had ten lean years. It is well recognized that the whole grain handling and transportation system needs to be renovated, and surely this is the segment of our industry that needs to be looked at. Could the minister reply?
Mr. Chairman, the simple answer is no, it does not qualify under the manufacturing and processing concept.
Would the minister consider the advisability of this? As was pointed out, manufacturing has had many good years whereas this industry has had a poor decade and really is in need of renovation.
Mr. Chairman, we are really talking about a different type of international competition here. There are other ways we have tried to help the grain producers of the country.

I should like to ask the minister a couple of questions. I was interested in his description of how difficult it is to define precisely what is processing and manufacturing and what is not. As I understood it, I think the minister said it was better not to try to bring down a precise definition as in many cases that would have to be left to the courts to decide. This is a little confusing to me since I listened to the minister's first budget on May 8, 1972 in which he said that the objective of the budget was to generate more economic activity and thereby generate more jobs. He hoped that manufacturers and processors would start then-and that is 14 months ago-in the knowledge that they could expect tax reductions on January 1 next, that is January 1, 1973, and start to expand their operations, thereby increasing employment.
People in business are not going to start on an expansive operation unless they know what the reward is going to be. Fourteen months have passed and I would have thought that in that time the minister and his department would have had to come to a very precise decision on
July 3, 1973

a very large number of cases, where people say, "Look, I do this: am I a manufacturer or processor or am I not? If I am, what percentage of my operation will be credited to being a manufacturer and processor, and to what extent can I expect a tax reduction on January 1, 1973?"
I am amazed to hear the minister state now that people may have to go to the courts and get a decision. This is a very lengthy process. How in the world can we expand our operations in business unless the government decides whether this tax reduction is to be made available to certain parts of the manufacturing community?

Let me put it this way to the hon. gentleman. I have said that it is more advantageous to the manufacturing and processing community to have a general definition. The marginal cases are probably fewer than 3 per cent to 4 per cent. These are cases where it is not clear whether the operation or part of the operation falls under head of manufacturing or processing. For the last 12 months, in expectation of parliament dealing with the matter, that 3 per cent or 4 per cent has been approaching the Department of National Revenue for rulings on whether, in an administrative sense, they qualify under the definition. Those rulings have been given to eliminate the uncertainty about which the hon. gentleman has been so concerned. I understand his concern. We have been trying to anticipate it and rulings are being given in advance of the passage of this legislation.
I am certainly glad to hear that because otherwise it would be very difficult to operate. The minister said that tax reductions were estimated to cost about a quarter of a billion dollars a year-
Half a billion.
The tax reductions alone?
Sorry; the two of them together.

I am dealing now with the tax reduction which in my calculation is $260 million a year. Would the minister not agree that businessmen who are given these tax reductions have three choices open to them: they can either expand their operations as the government wants them to, and that is beneficial; they can put the money into reserves if they want to; or they can pay the money out in dividends. Is this a fair statement of the case?
That is a fair statement of the case.

Then as I see it, the taxpayers of Canada are paying for this 100 per cent, because that $260 million is made available to manufacturers and processors through a tax reduction. That money must be made up by an additional charge on the other taxpayers of Canada and those taxes will not be made available for the general running of government and the nation, which cost a great deal of money as the minister knows only too well.
Now, you have the taxpayers of Canada making up that extra $260 million in a year. They know by the minister's own statement that there is only one chance in three that the money is going to be used as the minister and the
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
government want it to be used-to expand operations. Would the minister mind telling me this, instead of laughing the whole thing off and having a grand old time: Is this $260 million being charged to the taxpayers of Canada?
The minister is smiling. Apparently he thinks this is a huge joke, I want him to take this more seriously. Can he explain to the committee how he can justify this bill for $260 million in one year, when he knows there is only one chance in three that this money will be used to stimulate business? There is one chance in three that it will find its way into company reserves and one chance in three that it will be paid out as dividends to the shareholders of the corporations involved. Would he explain this, without laughing?

Mr. Chairman, if I was smiling, I was not smiling at the proposition. That is an interesting theory of probabilities. Apparently, because there are three choices open, the probability of one of them being fulfilled is one in three. That reasoning would not carry the hon. member far in any course on probability. There are three possibilities; that does not mean that there are three definite probabilities.
I would think that parliament would be observing and monitoring this whole process. After all, business, by definition, wants to expand, wants to remain competitive, wants to increase productive capacity and wants, as a Canadian operation, to ward off foreign competition, either abroad or in Canadian markets.
I suggest that increasing the cash flow by reason of the tax reduction will increase the prospects for investment, will increase the prospects for a legitimate return and for an expansion of productive capacity and facilities; and that, eventually, will lead to increased job potential in manufacturing concerns and, certainly, in secondary and tertiary industries, and particularly in service industries which depend on manufacturing concerns. I would think that if the motive of the private sector were a greater return, enhanced because of greater productive capacity- if that makes any sense at all-that motive will be fulfilled.
As I said on budget night, to which statement the hon. member referred, if business does not respond in the way that the government expects, namely with increased production facilities, competitive prices, more competitive prices leading to a preservation and enhancement of Canadian jobs, and an expansion of the whole employment base in this country, then, obviously, the country will be looking for a different minister of finance.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, the minister said very confidently that in one year's time we will know how this policy is working. Does he think it is sensible business practice to toss a gift of $260 million, money supplied by the Canadian taxpayer, to business? Does he think it is fair just to toss this gift into the lap of business and say, "I hope that your good sense will make you use this in a way we believe you should use it?" Has he any reason for

July 3, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
believing that the majority of businessmen would use the money as he wishes? Has he any guarantee, any assurance, that they will not use most of this money either for paying into their reserves or for paying out in dividends? Has he any assurance that the businessmen who, when he introduced this measure, might have slapped him on the back and said, "John you are the greatest, we are going to do exactly what you want", did not say behind his back, "Boy, we sure conned that guy?" I do not say that they did that, but they could have done it.
Does the Minister of Finance not think, before giving away $260 million of the taxpayers money, that he should have a proper assurance from the people with whom he is dealing as to what they are to do with that money? I should like to know from the minister if he feels that tossing this money into the laps of business, and giving it one year in which to do something, is satisfactory. Does he not think that it would have been better to make that money available to business, or even a great deal more money than that available, and say, "This is what we want you to do, and we will pay you in exact proportion to what you do. We will be much more generous than we have been in the past offers we have made, but we want to make sure that for every dollar we spend we get a dollar in return." Does he not think that business would listen to that proposition?
Mr. Chairman, I do not know how the hon. gentleman can reconcile his intervention tonight with the speeches he made when he was minister of trade and commerce.
I will answer that question, but you answer mine.
I think, after I get back to my office tonight, I will get out some of the hon. member's old speeches and send them back to him for his edification.

The minister obviously does not intend to answer my straightforward question, because he has no way of answering it. He is simply throwing this money, provided by the taxpayers of Canada, to business without any assurance that business will spend it in the way he wants.
Further, let me say this about my attitude when I was minister of trade and commerce. Every time a proposition was made to business, it was made on the basis that the proposal was to be lived up to or the money would not be paid. That is the basis on which we worked. I am glad the minister will read my speeches. Perhaps he will learn something about the business he is in. Perhaps he will learn the proper way to handle the taxpayers' money; obviously he is not doing that at present.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to pursue the questions of that great red Tory, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings. May I ask the Minister of Finance whether his department has undertaken studies which indicate that manufacturing companies will use the extra funds that will become available as a result of corporate tax cuts for further investment and, thus, for more job creation.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, we have received a great deal of information on a confidential basis regarding the investment plans of companies following passage of this bill. Actually, intentions to purchase equipment and plant have been augmented a good deal in the last six months. Businesses have anticipated passage of the bill. Let me say to the hon. gentleman and to the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings that part of the proof of the pudding is that between May 1972 and May 1973, 497,000 new jobs have been created in this country, a record that, if the hon. gentleman had been in office, we should have been reminded of every day.
Not at all. When I was in office everybody knew what was going on. We told people the facts in an honest, straightforward way. We would not need to remind the country.

I think the hon. gentleman must realize that this is a long-term structural change and is part of the series of industrial policies that this government is bringing before the country. Obviously it will take some time to see the full amplitude and effectiveness of this particular measure.
That is not an answer at all.

Mr. Chairman, I think the Minister of Finance should tell the committee the source of his information. I do not think it should be confidential. I think we should know on what he is basing his judgment.
Let me refer the Minister of Finance to one or two statistics which have to do with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. As the minister knows, in 1971-72 the corporations of this country saw their profits going up; yet, according to Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce statistics, new investment in manufacturing in this country actually went down in those two years.
In view of that information, how can the Minister of Finance suggest that if corporations gain extra funds as a result of the corporate tax cut, they will channel those funds into new investment? For example, in 1970, when corporate profits were at a much lower level, new investment in manufacturing, according to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, was at around $3,223 billion. Two years later, when profits had gone up considerably, corporate investment stood at around $2,956 billion, down several hundred million dollars. In light of that information, can the minister assure the committee that the new windfalls that will accrue to some corporations will necessarily be channeled into investment and, thus, into more job creation in the country?
I wish to ask the Minister of Finance-
Oh, oh!

I do not know whether the minister gets a lot of help from those behind him, but I hope he does. The minister speaks about the monitoring process and contemplates making a report shortly after April 1, 1974. Can the minister tell the House what he will be monitoring and what he will regard as a satisfactory performance
July 3, 1973

as a result of the proposal now before the House? What will be the ingredients of this performance? Can the minister tell us in a precise fashion what he anticipates will be a satisfactory result?
That's a good one.

The minister speaks about monitoring. He speaks about results. The committee is entitled to know what the minister is going to monitor, what he is going to be looking for and what he is going to regard, as of now at least, as a satisfactory performance as a result of these tax proposals.

Mr. Chairman, I can give the hon. gentleman a description of what we are going to monitor. As to whether the results are satisfactory or not, I will make two comments.
First, these are medium and long term measures. It will take some time in terms of the fulfillment of an industrial strategy to find out how effective they are. I am suggesting that in terms of the competitive fabric of world taxation systems and incentives that our competitors, particularly the United States, the common market and Japan are giving to their own manufacturers, this is a measure to maintain a competitive posture on behalf of Canadian business now and in the future, and for the protection of Canadian jobs.
My second comment is that whether these issues are working or not will be a matter for parliament to decide on the basis of the facts presented to it. The monitoring process will reveal a gradual process, gradual because it will take some time for the structural effect to be assessed in the Canadian economy.
In view of the priority of these corporate tax measures, work has been proceeding on the recording and review procedure to provide the basis for assessing the impact of the measures. The following activities will be undertaken in making this assessment. First, we will be looking for the direct impact of the measures. The direct impact that the measures have had on existing companies or are likely to have will be examined by means of a questionnaire survey and interviews. Questionnaires will be sent to about 1,000 manufacturers and processing corporations representing several times as many establishments. It will include representation from all industrial segments, all regions of the country and virtually all sizes of corporations. This mailing will include all the largest firms in the country as well as a number of smaller companies. Interviews will be held with the 200 largest firms and about 25 medium and 25 small manufacturing and processing companies.
We anticipate that the companies' response to the new tax measures will be motivated in part by their expectation of increased cash flows, but more importantly by a fundamental policy improvement designed to improve the investment climate in this country. For this reason, particular attention will be given to the ways in which the companies have been able to maintain and improve their competitive position in the domestic and international markets, making new investments and expanding their work forces. In addition, an assessment will be made of
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
their improved ability to withstand price increases or cause prices to be lowered.
To determine the extent to which the measures have promoted the establishment of entirely new ventures, we will rely largely on the considerable contact DREE and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce have with industry. In addition, we will make use of our own contacts with industry and maintain close watch on new plant announcements and other press releases.
We will also be looking for secondary effects. The secondary effects of the measures will be assessed in two ways. Extrapolation of the results of the mailings should enable us to estimate the impact of the measures on the entire manufacturing and processing sector. Through econometric modelling techniques, an assessment will be made of the secondary and subsequent effects on the economy in general. In addition, in the course of the interviews companies will be asked to furnish examples of specific instances where their actions have had secondary effects, on suppliers for example. These findings together with additional analyses, will form the basis for the interim report to be prepared early next year and tabled no latter than April 1, 1974. During 1974 another mailing will be made and another survey conducted. A final report will be prepared in late 1974 for presentation to the House for the end of the year.
Mr. Chairman, the attitude of the government toward the results of this measure will depend upon the interpretation that the corporations examined will place upon their decisions.

No, Mr. Chairman. It will depend partly on their reaction in subjective terms to the legislation and partly on the objective results that we find over a period of time as to how they have responded in terms of plant extension, new products, competitive pricing, international competition, piercing new markets and so on. It will be partly subjective in terms of their own assessment. After all, this depends on a subjective response of the community to the process and also on the objective returns from that response.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to push this too far, but has the minister any method of determining whether a decision as a result of this change is due to something else, bearing in mind of course that any company receiving the benefit of a tax cut will naturally wish to continue and therefore wish to ascribe as much as possible to the tax cut? Has the minister any objective method of really measuring the actual results of the tax cut as distinct from the results attributed to the tax cut by those who benefit from it?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member of course raises one of the fundamental problems in estimating the effect of any economic policy. What are the exact motivations and what weight does one attach to every single motive in capital investment or any individual business decision? It is very hard indeed to evaluate in individual cases, but taken over a larger sample, one would think that trends would appear.

July 3, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)

Mr. Chairman, I have a question following the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition. Is the minister in a position tonight to at least estimate, after this legislation has to all intents and purposes been in effect for six months now, what number of employees have actually gained employment as a result of the measures within this act?

No, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I cannot. Although some business decisions have already been made in anticipation of the passage of this legislation, a good many other business decisions are awaiting the bill's passage.

When I was questioning the Minister of Finance earlier, his deputy indicated some surprise at my suggestion that there may be many manufacturing and processing businesses that will not be able to get the full benefit of the 9 per cent reduction as a result of this proposed formula. I was wondering if the minister could be more specific. I refer to page 7 of the release put out by the minister in which he refers to essentially ancillary activity. There are three descriptive paragraphs on how his ML ingredient will function and how his MC ingredient will function. In the second paragraph, he says that the resulting figures for labour and capital in the enumerators of the formula will not be allowed to exceed their respective figures in the denominator. This adjustment will mean that a corporation which devotes at least 75 per cent of its labour and 85 per cent of its fixed capital directly to manufacturing and processing activities will receive the 40 per cent or 20 per cent tax rate. That is stated in the final paragraph. Is it not true that a corporation which cannot count on at least 75 per cent or, in the case of fixed capital, 85 per cent, will not be able to get the full benefit of the tax reduction inasmuch as it is responsible for a cost which it is not able to charge within the formula?

That is true. There are two reasons. First, there is an allocation formula, except for small business, which limits the tax rate to that income derived under the formula from processing and manufacturing-not just direct costs for labour or fixed assets, but also a certain amount of indirect cost by way of the larger enumerator over the smaller denominator, 100 over 75; this is where we get the figures 75 per cent and 85 per cent. To the extent that a corporation derives its income from manufacturing and processing it gets the entire reduction. To the extent that other sources of income are part of its total income, then on its total income the reduction would fall short.

With regard to another statement which appears in the release on page six under "Total Fixed Capital", could the minister elaborate on paragraph two in which he states that the cost of fixed capital must be reduced to an annual cost comparable to the annual labour cost. The release says:
The annual cost of fixed capital will be an approximation of the annual cost of the funds necessary to acquire those depreciable assets. This will be obtained by multiplying the original cost of each depreciable asset owned by 10 per cent.

Take the example of a corporation which bought an estate for $100,000 several years ago. Its resale today would be, say, $1 million. Perhaps the company has mortgaged it during the interval. Would it be able to claim only 10 per cent of the original $100,000?

Yes, of course, because that is the whole basis for a capital cost on a fixed asset in any event. I think the hon. gentleman will understand that against the original cost, from which capital cost is computed, 10 per cent is a pretty generous allowance.

A question with respect to monitoring the effectiveness of this legislation. The minister told us earlier that mining companies, for example, already receive certain incentives under the tax legislation by way of depreciation allowances, fast write-offs, deferred taxes and so on. I am wondering how effective the minister's proposals will be in terms of job creation. Take INCO as an example. In 20 months its work force fell from 18,000 to 13,000. If one of the primary objectives of a favourable tax system is to stimulate employment, how effective are the incentives presently offered likely to be when it comes to creating new jobs?

I hope the hon. member will forgive me if I do not get into actual situations affecting individual companies. The fact remains that under this system of which the hon. gentleman complains this country put together 100,000 more jobs in real terms than the entire industrial complex of Europe, and has in the past year, added 497,000 new jobs to the industrial complex of this country. So the system must have something in its favour.

I was interested to hear the answer the minister gave to the Leader of the Opposition regarding the kind of report he would seek from manufacturers and processors a year from now. The answer he read off- obviously something which came out of the department- referred to a series of vague and general questions, such as "Do you think this has been a good thing?" or "Could you tell us how it has helped you to become more effective?", and so on. Obviously, all those who received this questionnaire will answer in general terms, saying how grand the idea has been, since there is no human being who does not like a tax reduction. They will all say; "Dear Mr. Minister, this has been a grand thing, very helpful to our business. Please issue another cheque as soon as you can because we like this nice free money, it is very helpful for the various uses we have in mind: some of it could be higher dividend payments, another part could be used to place more money in our reserves," and so on.
When the minister addresses his questions to the processors and manufacturers next year, does he intend to ask them specifically how they spent the money they received? Does he intend to ask them for a strict accounting of how much was received, how much was spent on expanding operations, increasing research and development, increasing productivity and so on? Does he intend to ask them to report on the increase in their activities and on the new employment created by the company as a result of the concession? Does he intend to carry out a survey to ascertain how many of the 497,000 new jobs of
July 3, 1973

which he spoke, came from the people who were told 14 months ago that they would get this tax reduction, and who could therefore be expected to move ahead and do some of the things the minister wanted them to do, and ascertain what proportion came from people to whom he gave no tax reduction? Has the hon. gentleman made a survey in the last six months to see how things are going, and does he intend to have a definitive answer ready when he makes his report to parliament a year from now?

As I said to the Leader of the Opposition, I suppose it would be hard to isolate all the factors which influence business decisions and decide what weight to attach to each. The hon. gentleman knows that a good many business decisions will depend not only on this proposal but on the international trade climate, the monetary situation, the collective market psychology, the effect of an inflationary situation, the efforts of the United States administration to re-assert leadership in economic affairs-
And the weather. Don't forget the weather.

I will not, and neither should the hon. gentleman, because the weather is very important both in his constituency and in mine. No one can neglect the weather. The hon. member may not agree, but it is the disastrous harvests in parts of Asia, North America and elsewhere which have contributed to the high cost of food. He may not agree, but I am telling him that it happens to be the case. We are attempting, through this monitoring service, to assess these criteria, recognizing that it may be somewhat hard to pinpoint the precise effect of each.
In terms of subjective criteria we will be looking at employment, prices, new facilities and new market penetration, as I told the Leader of the Opposition. In terms of subjective criteria I am surprised at the hon. gentleman denigrating that, because he was one of the best subjective ministers I can remember.
You can't fight that, John.

The hon. member understands that investment depends on a climate of confidence and the anticipation of reasonable prospects for the country and reasonable returns. He understood the collective psychology of the marketplace, and I am surprised that because he is sitting on the other side of the House he forgets some of the fundamental commonsense he exuded when on this side.

On this last occasion when I will rise I will just say that having asked a number of straightforward questions I have received no answers at all, just a lot of guff. I think we can all be sure that the minister's meeting with businessmen a year from now will be a replay of the first meeting. They will get together and everybody will say: "John, it has been great. You sure helped us. The tax reduction was wonderful. We have confidence and we are going ahead. All you have to do, John, as soon as you get back is to write us another cheque and everybody will be
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
happy." And "John" will go away thinking he has done the greatest job of any finance minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I do not know who this "John" is to whom the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings is referring, but if he happens to be the Minister of Finance, I think a more appropriate designation by title should be made.

Mr. Chairman, the last time I rose on this matter was to direct a question to the minister on the definitions in sub-paragraph (vi) of sub-clause (3), which refers to processing to the prime metal stage. The minister indicated that the mining industry is already covered in respect of depletion and exploration allowances. I suggested that may be a satisfactory explanation for sub-paragraph (v) concerning the extracting of minerals from a mineral resource, but it does not explain the processing to prime metal.
I refer the minister to a situation where pelletized iron ore, which is certainly not a prime metal, is sent to the smelter. Surely the smelting operation is refining to prime metal, and the existing tax laws give no particular relief in respect of that item. There is no question that there may be excessive depletion allowances and excessive exploration allowances in some people's view, but the question really is whether there should not be some incentive to operations geared to processing or refining the raw materials in this country in order that we have more jobs in the refining or metal processing fields. Surely this particular sub-paragraph should be removed from the bill.

I want to reassure the hon. gentleman that both stages excluded from this particular incentive, namely those suggested under (v) and (vi), are covered by the existing incentives for mining and oil, particularly in (vi) which refers to those called "production profits" against which depletion allowances can be claimed.

Covered and recovered.
[ Translation]

Mr. Chairman, we are listening to a very interesting discussion. However, I would like to know on what is based the minister's assertion that many jobs will be created if the proposed 9 per cent tax cut was achieved during 1973. And what surprises me is that he said afterwards that we should wait for some time before knowing whether these measures will work out well. This is staggering. They must believe or not believe in this measure!
What are the minister's advisers doing in all this business? Are they advising the minister simply because of their experience or do they do so with competence? The people, I suggest, have had enough of this advice given by senior officials to cabinet members. They make experiments, then they say: Well, we failed, but we do not offer any alterative. And taxpayers must endure the effect of these unfortunate experiments. I guess that these public servants are paid a salary high enough to be able to give sound advice to the minister. Is it true that this will create employment or is it false? Well, we will only know it after one year of trial, which staggers me.

July 3, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
When I was secretary-treasury of a municipality and worked at the preparation of a municipal budget, it did not happen often that our forecasts rang false by the end of the year. I understand that we have a larger ship here, but the people are also paid more than simple secretaries of municipalities, because they must have more experience. They are university graduates. They have some value or they do not have any.
Therefore it is my firm opinion, Mr. Chairman, that we are entitled this evening to ask the minister to tell us what the basis is for his statment to the House that the tax reduction wil help create jobs. Are these new jobs that are going to be added to those now existing? Are we sure that these corporations will not use these tax exemptions to modernize their enterprises, or that at the end of the year, it will not help reduce the number of jobs because of modernization? These are all questions we must ask ourselves seriously if we are to know where we are headed.
In all seriousness, I would like to ask the minister to explain to the committee the basis for proposing such a measure. Is sufficient data available to be able to say: This will give such and such a result. In that event, if a certain result is to be achieved, I can understand that there might be a certain margin of error, but it is a different matter to say: it will take some time before we know whether the results will be good. Imagine a doctor advising a patient that he needs a blood transfusion, in the hope that it will do him some good, and then saying to him: We will try it, then we'll see!
Mr. Chairman, I think that we have quite enough serious problems in Canada. Unemployed people waiting for jobs and wanting to make a real contribution, by working, by doing something. This is either going to create jobs or it isn't. As a member of the committee, I would like to know how far we can go in this direction, with assurance, so that it can help create jobs, and on what basis.

Perhaps the Minister of Finance wishes to reply to the hon. member for Bellechasse.

Mr. Chairman, I always listen with interest to the comments of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) and I think I know his philosophy; he has some confidence in private industry.
One of the factors of private industry is that if you allow for an increase in funds, you then favour capital investment and production facilities. By doing so, you eventually promote new employment, new jobs within the corporation itself as a manufacture or in other industries whose prosperity depends on that manufacture. If the hon. member has confidence in the system, he has already answered his question.
Mr. Chairman, I agree with the answer of the minister, but my second point is this:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I will return to the hon. member for Bellechasse in a moment. The hon. member for Peel South.

I want to ask the minister two or three other questions in connection with the specifically excluded industries. Why is it that those persons who produce electrical energy or steam for sale are excluded as manufacturers or processors whereas, I presume, a company that produces electricity or steam for use in its own operation is able to have the lower tax rate? It strikes me as rather peculiar that in a day when we are talking about energy shortages those who produce electric energy or steam for same are excluded from any allowance as manufacturers or processors. I refer to the kind of thing that is likely to develop in my constituency where people involved in getting rid of pollutants are in the process of organizing the sale of steam to neighbouring industries, and presumably that is a good thing to promote and develop; but this bill says that if you produce steam or electricity and sell it, you get no particular allowance.
Another thing that I found strange was with respect to the distribution of gas. Presumably if you distribute gas in operating a private utility as opposed to a public utility, or just distribute gas for your own purposes, you may well have an allowance as a manufacturer or processor; but if you happen to do it as a public utility or on behalf of others for sale, you are excluded. Can the minister explain to me and to the committee the reason for that?

Primarily the reason is that in the case of public utilities, they are established by the province or the federal government and for that reason they are not subject to the international competitive price structure or to the international direct impact of foreign competition.
The hon. gentleman mentioned pollution. There are already incentives in the Income Tax Act providing for accelerated depreciation against equipment purchased for anti-pollutant purposes.
[ Transla tion]

Mr. Chairman, I would also like to ask the minister, in view of the statement made by him a moment ago, if we will have to wait a while before knowing if those measures will give, the results hoped for. Since it is a matter of mathematics it seems to me that it would be easy to get an answer. If the tax reduction is in the whereabouts of, let us say, $500 million and that amount is actually invested and not cashed in to the benefit of shareholders, in order to produce expansion and create jobs, it should be possible to say today that it will produce a specific result. So I think that we should not have to wait a year to say that it will produce a given result. We should be receiving today an answer as correct as possible to the effect that it will produce a specific result.
I think that we are entitled to ask and receive an answer.

I suppose, Mr. Chairman, that if the business does not use those funds to expand, to improve its production facilities in a field where competition is so rigorous, so brutal, particularly from the United States, Europe and Japan, it will not survive.
July 3, 1973

Mr. Chairman, in the same line of thought as the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) I would like to direct a question to the minister.
Let us imagine, for example, that 50 per cent of those industries which will have those benefits available to them reinvest those amounts of money to generate additional jobs but that, on the other hand, it is also proven that 50 per cent will not do so. What would then be the position of the government?
Mr. Chairman, that question is hypothetical; the result must be considered and it will be the duty of Parliament to do the same. We will be back on it in coming months.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance.
I should like to ask him what the difference is between a bill that grants a 9 per cent tax reduction to the corporations, and one that increases interest rates, to make up for the tax reduction, if not more. I wonder where the solution lies in that.
In one clause, the bill offers certain advantages, but in others it cancels them. I wonder where we are going, and I ask the minister to tell us, for the manufacturers borrow capital in huge quantities. Because they do, interest rates go up. So, I ask the minister to tell us what the advantages of this bill are.

Mr. Chairman, there are two aspects to the problem; first of all, we must consider the tax reduction from 49 to 40 per cent in relation to the 1 per cent increase in the rate of interest, half of which is tax deductible to balance that; then, if a given company has more investment money at its disposal because of the tax reduction, it can then limit its demand for loans.

The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) asked a while ago to the minister what were the real projections as to the 9 per cent tax reduction granted to corporations. We know that Mr. Benson's budget authorized a 1 per cent tax reduction to corporations as a result of which the minister would be in a position to say, with the support of statistics, whether the measure would have created employment or if at least it would have help preserve jobs.
Now, as the minister pointed out a while ago, it is rather difficult to say whether the measure can create employment, because it is merely a hypothetical issue. However, according to statistics, even if it did not create employment it has surely contributed to preserve jobs which normally would have been eliminated for lack of government intervention.
Now, according to those statistics based on the 1 per cent reduction granted in the previous budget of Mr. Benson, can the minister tell us whether there is a valid reason to increase again the deductions by 9 per cent?

I don't believe so, Mr. Chairman, especially since there is always a lapse of time between the introduction of an economic policy and its impact, and this delay is underestimated not only by
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
economists, I think, but also by newspapermen and politicians.
One must also consider that there were several consecutive budgets and I believe that in the present circumstances it would be very difficult to identify the effects of one budget in particular, among those of 1969, 1970 and 1971.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I know the minister is anxious to get this legislation through-
I am at the disposition of the Committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not saying that in any sense of criticism. He has been very generous with his explanations. They have not always been good explanations, in fact some were pretty awful, but he has been perfectly willing to give them. I am now going to test him with one or two questions and I am sure that, with the advice he will be receiving from his officials, he will be able to answer them immediately.
With respect to the definitions, he has taken the unique approach that instead of saying what processing and manufacturing are he has drafted the subclause to say what they are not.
That is not the first time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Taken with subclause (3) (a), in which the income of a corporation which has carried on business is taken into account by rules and regulations prescribed by the minister to determine its profits, these two provisions give quite a lot of scope to the minister, and he will probably need a lot of scope before he is finished. But why is there the exclusion of farming and fishing? I am not relating this to farmers particularly, although God knows they need the help, but rather to the type of processing and manufacturing that takes place, on a secondary or tertiary basis, of farm products.
I was not in the chamber earlier, and the minister may have answered this already. I was with his colleague in the other house where we were trying to expedite the business of the House, in spite of the obstacles, in spite of the sand thrown in the machinery by those on the other side.

Mr. Chairman, with deference to the hon. member for Peace River may I say that we did go into this subject with some amplitude earlier in the evening. Basically we are leaving the definition to the general dictionary definition of business and manufacturing, and of those words as understood by the accounting and business professions, subject to exclusions, to make it clear that we are dealing not with the primary resources and the service sector but with manufacturing and processing, upon which there can be the most immediate impact of the pressures of world competition. That is the general philosophy of it. It is not the first time that

July 3, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
something is defined, particularly in the Income Tax Act, by way of exclusion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am thinking in particular of the north country, the northern parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta. The farmers up there have been told to grow wheat, then not to grow wheat, and now they have been told to grow it again. I know that if this government is still in power for another year they will probably be told not to grow wheat again. They have been told that land should be put into grass, and later told it should be taken out of grass, and so on.
A number of farmers in the north country did get together over the last year or two, and with their own funds and some assistance, guided by the intelligence which the Lord has given them and which has been sharpened by living in the north country, they have established pelletizing plants, rapeseed crushing plants, and so on. These are private organizations, not co-operatives at all, and it seems to me there should be a very good reason for excluding them.
To take the rapeseed process one step further, they convert it into crude oil, which is the crushing, and then it is mixed with other substances to make a cooking oil. That is the tertiary process.

Mr. Chairman, I said earlier that I would not want to get into the position of interpreting and pronouncing on individual situations. Anyway the hon. gentleman knows that whatever I say on the floor of this committee is not necessarily going to bind a court, except to give an indication of the intention of the minister.
I would point out to the hon. member that the Minister of National Revenue is already giving advance rulings on whether individual situations qualify within the definition of manufacturing and processing. Certainly in the agricultural and fishing fields the conversion of grain and fish into a type of substance by way of pelletizing, or processing of the fish, would qualify under the definition of processing. We have already made that clear to a number of concerns right across the country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: But the minister is not precisely ruling out a rapeseed crushing plant.
I am not the world's greatest authority on that type of plant, so I am certainly not ruling it out.

Mr. Chairman, further to the question raised by the hon. member for Peace River, there are a number of alfalfa pellet plants, and in this process' the reduction of the product is very closely intergrated. I would ask the minister whether such an operation would fit into the definition of processing as it appears in the bill?

Here again, I really have not got the factual background to answer this question. However, if it is within that general concept of processing that I described to the hon. member for Peace River, it would; but the hon. gentleman, on behalf of his constituents, should get a more precise ruling, on the basis

of the factual situation he describes, from my colleague the Minister of National Revenue.

Mr. Chairman, the point on which I seek an explanation from the minister for clarification purposes is a rather complicated one, in that first of all it arises out of the fact that regulations are going to be made on recommendations of the minister regarding the definition of income from manufacturing and processing, which however excludes-and I refer to subparagraph (x) at line 22 on page 4-any manufacturing or processing in which less than 10 per cent of its gross revenues are derived from manufacturing and processing of goods for sale or lease.
In other words, 10 per cent or more of the gross revenues must be from the permitted activities under paragraphs (A) and (B), but then going on to subclause (4) on page 5, there is permitted to be added to whatever may be the active business, or principal activity of the company, a proportion of gross revenue arising from am activity that such corporation carries on in partnership with others. I put it to the minister that there are such circumstances, let us say in the manufacture and leasing of machinery in partnership with other corporations; it may be an offshore operation, which is permissible, and which is very lucrative from the point of view of Canadian business. But whereas there may have been substantial gross revenues in the particular year, there may have been extraordinary losses or costs imposed upon it as a result of which the net income is very low-as a matter of fact it might even be negative-and the company has not been able, on that basis, to apportion to itself the appropriate proportion of gross revenues from the partnership operations. Therefore it finds itself disqualified under (x).
I put this case before the minister not to have a definitive answer, unless he has it here, but for consideration in the formulation of the regulations for the determination of income. I think there are a number of Canadian specialty firms making very sophisticated machinery, say in oil field work, in construction and many other activities, where its activity is conducted offshore. This is something that I think we should attempt to preserve, and that the proportion of the gross revenue from the partnership operation should not be exclusively related to the proportion of the income from the partnership operation. I think there should be an alternative, although I am in no position to indicate precisely what it might be. It might be, shall we say, on the basis of the partnership interest-that if company A owns a 25 per cent interest in the partnership, it can allocate to the gross revenues of its active business 25 per cent of the gross revenues of the partnership operation, when these might be an alternative, rather than net income. I think one can get into difficulty with this.
I think we will go over that point and look into it. To the moment I have not received any submissions, but we will look into it.

I hope I am not setting up a straw man in order to knock it down. It seems to me there is here a conceivable operation, and one would not want the regulations to be so tight that there would not be
July 3, 1973

the maximum scope for Canadian business. I hope under the Income Tax Act-and this was a fundamental principle certainly that I advocated-that there will be no unnecessary obstacle put before Canadian business competing abroad.

Mr. Chairman, when I was raising some points with the Minister of Finance earlier I touched on this question of the total fixed capital and how his formula proposed to deal with it, and I proposed to ask a further question when the hon. member for Nickel Belt interceded. I was wondering if the minister would indicate, as I believe he agrees, that my interpretation of his page 6 summation of this item is correct-whether it has the net effect of increasing or lowering the rate to the corporation which subsequently will receive the tax reduction contemplated by this bill.

Mr. Chairman, I think it has a neutral effect as it applies to fixed capital because it applies to the enumerator of the equation and the denominator. The enumerator as it applies to the operation is directly related to the manufacturing and processing part and the denominator to the entire operation of a firm, so it cancels out. It is neutral in its application.

All I can say is that I am very interested in that answer. I hope the Minister of Finance is correct, as that is not my understanding from one of his professional advisers.
To go on to another point, earlier the Minister of Finance indicated that he felt that a rough estimate of the number of foreign corporations or perhaps the larger foreign corporations that will benefit from this act would amount to about 60 per cent of the total number that will actually receive a benefit. I was wondering if the minister could indicate in what way he was able to reconcile the benefit he appears to be conferring on those foreign corporations with the effect that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce feels that his bill C-132 would have concerning the screening of foreign companies that might wish to set up business in future in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I do not see any problem of reconcilation there. My concern at the moment is that, since the fundamental purpose of the legislation is to protect the manufacturing and processing jobs, we have to enhance that potential against world competition here and abroad. Since foreign-owned corporations contribute about half those jobs, we have to continue to move forward to better control of our own economy and resources, and to add a base that does not risk the immediate job potential. I see no difficulty in reconciling these propositions.

Are we to understand that the minister in effect in saying that foreign corporations within the country, provided that they create employment, are, to use the reference of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, of significant benefit to the country, whereas those that may be coming in will have to be screened to ensure that they are of significant benefit?

That is a normal situation; I am not saying that or denying that. Obviously the
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
definition of "significant benefit" includes employment potential among its factors. What I am saying is that my immediate job is to try and enhance and protect the job potential of the country That is the purpose of the bill.

Coming back to the actual definition of manufacturing and processing which is the main part of clause (3) which we have been considering, I was wondering if the minister or his deputy would have any comment for the committee concerning an area such as data processing. I notice in the press release that they specifically exclude wages with respect to data processing as a cost in determining income. I was wondering if the minister could indicate whether he felt that the data processing firm itself would be clearly a manufacturer or processor who would have the benefit of the act.
Yes, subject to whatever interpretation my colleagues would give to it. I would think it is primarily a service industry.
