On subclause (2)

The effect of subclause (2) as it appears on page 5 is to keep the open-ended nature of the tax deduction allowed on corporate profits arising out of manufacturing and processing.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, the party of which I am a member has taken the position that this type of deduction should not be a permanent feature of our tax system. The Leader of the Opposition and other spokesmen of my party have suggested that we should place a limit on this during the year 1973 because, as the result of the budget of May, 1972, it was obvious that businesses which should otherwise qualify under this act took action. They based their decisions and operations on the word of the minister. They, therefore, may have committed themselves, and it was only equitable that at least these provisions should be effective for this year, so that what they had committed themselves to during 1972 and in the early part of 1973 could be carried out.
We fur.her said that some businesses during the fiscal year 1973 would enter into firm commitments to receive equipment, particularly equipment that was to be paid for

July 3, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
over a longer term. We said we would do this, because if we go into accelerated capital cost allowances, we will find that the definition of manufacturing and processing, under the regulations provided for in the section of block three which we have discussed will form the basis for the order in council that will be passed by the government, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, dealing with capital cost allowances. Therefore, these are inextricably tied together. We felt that commitments for the purchase of machinery and equipment during the 1973 fiscal year would need to be honoured.
It may be said, why do we not object to this particular clause? In order to mesh with subclause (3), which appears at the top to page 6 and in which a review process is provided for with regard to March 31, 1974, one must say this: if this is to be at all meaningful, one must include the words, "and subsequent years after 1973". It is for this reason that this part establishes the nature of the review process.
The minister is to propose an amendment which will not alter the heart and core of that review process but will make modifications to it that, I hope, will meet the views of the official opposition in that connection. In any event, as I said at the opening of the debate this afternoon, there is no way that one can expect these tax cuts, which affect a limited segment of Canadian industry and do not affect all Canadian industry, to become a permanent feature of the tax system. So we took our position, and I think it is a perfectly logical position, as the minister himself recognized.
In the budget of May 8, 1972, the accelerated capital cost allowances, as proposed, were open ended as to time. That was not the case in the February 19, 1973 budget, when the minister introduced the two year limitation. His two year proposal, in view of the commitments that have been made in 1973, is not far different from ours in essence. I remember the hon. member for York South applauding on budget night when the minister proposed to review capital cost allowances, and so on. This review process was proposed, but it was not something that had been proposed on the night of the budget. I am referring to the review after March 31, 1974. It need not be a single, annual review. It can be repeated, under the provisions of the legislation, on the basis of information that is available either from the government monitoring service or from other sources.
I do not apologize for the questions that were asked by members of the opposition and members of other parties with regard to the monitoring service. They were to test its probity and the minister's understanding, and were to elicit an elaboration in detail of that monitoring service so that the interim report to be brought down in April, 1974 may be of some utility. I do not know how great its value will be.
Certainly, we will look forward to a good and comprehensive report, which the minister has undertaken will be filed by March 31, 1974. It will be filed, I am sure, with the monitoring service, if this whole tax legislation is still in operation and if this monitoring service is in operation. It will be reporting and will make information available not only to the government but to outside sources. The opposition, whatever it may be at the time, will have information

available to it which could trigger off, if need be, the review process provided for in subclause (3).
That is why we say that subclause (2) in its present form does not negate but actually establishes the base for the review process and also the monitoring process that the government has undertaken to carry on with regard to this provision and other capital cost allowances that will apply to industry.

TRANSPORT-ALLEGED PLANNED FREIGHT RATE INCREASE IN ATLANTIC PROVINCES BY CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REQUEST THAT MINISTER TAKE STEPS TO PREVENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am overwhelmed by the influx of my colleagues who have come here this evening to hear my address.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: TRANSPORT-ALLEGED PLANNED FREIGHT RATE INCREASE IN ATLANTIC PROVINCES BY CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REQUEST THAT MINISTER TAKE STEPS TO PREVENT
speechtext: Order, please. Would hon. members please resume their seats. The hon. member for Hillsborough has the floor.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-ALLEGED PLANNED FREIGHT RATE INCREASE IN ATLANTIC PROVINCES BY CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REQUEST THAT MINISTER TAKE STEPS TO PREVENT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was paying tribute to my colleagues who are rushing back to hear my evening deliberations. On June 11 I asked the Minister of Transport the following question:
... It is based on a statement by Lome Mitton of the Atlantic provinces Transportation Commission to the effect that the CNR is planning a large freight rate increase and a change in demurrage rules which, according to the Commission, will cause undue hardship in Atlantic Canada. Has the minister been made aware of these deplorable proposals, and what steps has he in mind to forestall what would be the tenth freight rate increase in Atlantic Canada in the last four years?
July 3, 1973

He replied:
There was no general increase in freight rates in the Maritimes. There might be some specific increases. I can inquire and see to what extent there has been and make a report to the hon. gentleman some time this week.
I had to remind the minister that there had in fact been nine increases in four years. A week later I asked him further:
Has the minister received from the Premier of Prince Edward Island and or the other Atlantic premiers protests against the outrageous increase in freight rates announced by the CNR and, if so, what was his response to these hon. gentlemen?
He replied:
I do not remember having received any telegram worded in the way the hon. gentleman mentioned.
On a matter of such compelling importance as transportation, I am amazed that any political leaders in the Atlantic region would regard the subject with anything other than extreme concern. Nor can I understand why the proposed freight rate increase would not have been a major item on the agenda of the meeting which the minister held with the premiers of the four eastern provinces. What the Atlantic region needs is not a freight increase but a decrease.
On July 1, just two days ago, we in Prince Edward Island celebrated the centenary of our entrance into confederation. A major if not the major issue in the negotiations which preceded our joining the dominion concerned transportation.
Through all the years since, along with our sister provinces by the eastern seas, PEI has been troubled and injured by the transportation policies of the national government. Commissions, investigations, subsidies have brought some amelioration but still the problem lingers, still our economic growth is held back. Being on the extremity of the transportation link, it is not surprising that this should be the case. We must get our goods to market cheaply and expeditiously. The manufactured products of the affluent centre of the country should not arrive in our area with an excessive write-up resultant from burdensome freight rates.
It has always been my belief that while the DREE programs can be helpful, it would be far sounder economics for the federal government to assist the region in areas of its own economic advantage. For instance, PEI is enjoying a rapidly expanding tourist trade. People in the industry are doing well in coping with the increased influx. Eastern Provincial Airways has given us the finest direct service from Montreal, but the Department of Transport, which might have been expected to give the fullest possible boost to a local industry which is expending and expansive, has been slow to upgrade the Charlottetown airport to the standing which the traffic of today, to say nothing of tomorrow, warrants.
In my view, the transportation issue, always of concern, requires a new look with the most urgent priority. I rejoice that the government has discovered the west and I hope that despite the blunderings of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), the forthcoming meeting will be fruitful.
Adjournment Debate
However, I wonder why there was not a meeting of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with the premiers of the Atlantic provinces. Because our problems are of long duration is no reason why we should be expected to rest easily with them.
Certainly, on this projected freight rate boost we will not be complaisant. I urge the minister to not only contact the provincial people, but also to give leadership himself to prevent this further blow to our regional economy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-ALLEGED PLANNED FREIGHT RATE INCREASE IN ATLANTIC PROVINCES BY CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REQUEST THAT MINISTER TAKE STEPS TO PREVENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say to the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) that the minister and the government are concerned with all regions, not only Prince Edward Island.
The minister reviewed the agreed charge and demurrage increases in a letter to the hon. member dated June 13. This was after the hon. member asked his question in the House. Canadian railways have given notice that they will increase agreed charges for all contracts which are one year old on September 1, 1973, by 6 per cent, and on other contracts when they become one year old. These contracts may be terminated by either side on three months written notice. Agreed charges are low-contract rates voluntarily agreed to by shippers and railways in return for which the shippers agreed to ship a stated percentage of their traffic by rail.
Shippers affected by the increases have a number of options. They can agree to the increased rates, they can ship by rail under the regular open tariff rates, or by other modes of transport, such as trucks; they can use their own trucks. But there is no general increase in freight rates anticipated in the maritimes.
Furthermore, it should be noted that under the Transport Act, after an agreed charge has been in effect for three months, any association or other body representative of shippers in any locality can complain to the minister that an agreed charge discriminates unjustly against a shipper or places his business at an unfair disadvantage. In such circumstances, the minister can refer the complaints to the Canadian Transport Commission for investigation.
With reference to demurrage charges, these are tariffs designed not to produce revenue but rather to impose a penalty so as to prevent shippers from using railway cars for storage. The railways gave notice that they would reduce free time for loading from 38 hours to 24 hours by July 1, 1973 in order to increase utilization of railway equipment. No changes in demurrage rates are proposed and I should stress that these charges can be quite flexible in special cases.
Just two weeks ago, the minister announced that the federal-provincial committee on Atlantic region transportation is making good progress toward finalizing recommendations for selective increases in west-bound freight rate subsidies. These increases would aid Atlantic region shippers east of Quebec City. The federal-provincial committee itself stated that the increased subsidies should apply to commodities manufactured in the Atlantic region as wall as to fishery and agricultural products.

July 3, 1973

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-NORTHERN ONTARIO-GOVERNMENT ACTION FOLLOWING DISCUSSIONS WITH PROVINCIAL MINISTERS AND OFFICIALS
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-NORTHERN ONTARIO-GOVERNMENT ACTION FOLLOWING DISCUSSIONS WITH PROVINCIAL MINISTERS AND OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 11 I asked the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) a question with respect to action on the part of the government in relation to economic developments in Northern Ontario. The minister replied that discussions were underway between federal and provincial officials in connection with economic developments in the region.
Last Friday, June 29, the minister tabled a document entitled "Ontario: Economic Circumstances and Opportunities". This report on regional development affecting my part of the country is shallow and prejudicial; it reinforces the long-held colonialist view that the residents of Northern Ontario are condemned forever to be hewers of wood and drawers or water while their resources, both material and human, are shipped out to enrich other parts of the country and of the world.
In his comments at the end of the report the minister says: "I do not believe in instant solutions." Well, Mr. Speaker, he need have no fear on that score, because we in Northern Ontario have waited a long time to hear the federal government's position on regional development and we cannot but compare the time taken for this report to be prepared and tabled with the qestation period of the Asiatic elephant. That animal takes 22 months to deliver a calf, whereas this report took 100 years in the making but produced only a big fat zero. In other words, it is a nothing report. The minister says this is a working paper. Well, the fool in Shakespeare's Lear said: "Nothing will come of nothing."
The report makes out that Northern Ontario has a narrow economic base, slow employment growth, below average incomes and a high emigration rate. The report admits that the slow rate of population growth in northern Ontario is due mainly to the lack of employment opportunities, which has also caused rising unemployment and reduced income.
In a classic example of "pin the tail on the donkey" Liberal analysis, we find the report speaking of the hardships visited upon those areas of northern Ontario which were completely dependent upon a single resource, namely the gold mining areas. With the depletion of the ore reserves came the demise of the gold towns.
The report then goes on to say that despite increasing competition from alternate sources of supply in Canada and abroad, substantial output increases in mining, forestry and related manufacturing will probably occur, but- and I repeat, but-the employment gains will be small. In addition the report talks about prohibitive transportation costs and the uncertainty experienced as a result of mineral resource depletion in single-industry towns.
In the face of their own documentation of these problems, what does this report propose as solutions? For one, it proposes that there be a further expansion in the extraction and the processing of resources indigenous to the region. In other words, we are to let our non-renewable

resources be ripped from under our feet in the same manner that gold was ripped from under the feet of the gold mining towns. Indeed, while admitting to increasing competition from alternate sources of supply in Canada and abroad, there is no mention of the fact that much of this competition will come from the very multi-national corporations located in northern Ontario and presently engaged in the business of exploiting our resources.
Another so-called solution is the increase in the service industries associated with the growth of the major urban areas. The statement is made that urbanization itself is a job-creating industry. I ask, when there are no jobs, when there are no people, how will urbanization occur?
The report suggests-and this is incredible-that northern Ontario commence the exploitation and utilization of our abundant recreational resources. Now we are asked not only to deplete our mineral resources for shipment to southern Ontario and other countries where jobs are produced as a result of our labour, and not only are we asked to accelerate the chopping down of our forests, but we are slated to become southern Ontario's very own giant hot dog stand.
The report blatantly proposes tourism for northern Ontario, not simply as a solution to our problems, but as an accommodation to the people in southern Ontario where, as the report states, people are earning more money and finding that they have more time to devote to leisure activities.
It is clearly obvious that this report was written by individuals who have never set foot in northern Ontario and who view our area from a safe distance behind an Ottawa desk.
I offer eleven alternatives for regional development in northern Ontario. These are viable and completely within federal jurisdiction, and many of them have been concurred in by the Ontario provincial government. These alternatives are as follows: A permanent secretariat for regional development in northern Ontario; a regulatory agency within the secretariat to ensure long-range conservation and skilful exploitation of our non-renewable resources; a Crown corporation should be established for direct public investment in ventures in which private investors for one reason or another will not enter; designated special areas, a vehicle for establishing the proper infrastructure for the location of industrial parks in northern Ontario; incentives to the residents of northern Ontario in a graduated tax system declining as one moved into the designated area; disincentives for other wealthier parts of the province; selective transport and freight rate subsidies which should be co-ordinated with provincial carriers; the development of the growth centre complex for northern Ontario communities; direct government funding for municipalities in northern Ontario to develop cultural and social dimensions; co-ordinated air transport and communications systems throughout northern Ontario; and wherever incentive grants are made to corporations equity must be taken by the people of Canada, with no grants to foreign-owned companies.
These are proposed to the minister in all sincerity. In addition, I have invited him to visit northern Ontario on July 21 to meet and answer the questions of the people of northern Ontario.
July 3, 1973

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-EASTERN ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR AID TO FARMERS BECAUSE WET CONDITIONS PROHIBIT PLANTING OF CROPS
AGRICULTURE-EASTERN ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR AID TO FARMERS BECAUSE WET CONDITIONS PROHIBIT PLANTING OF CROPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 14, 1973, as recorded at page 4757 of Hansard, I directed a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), who I am pleased to see is in the House tonight, concerning the desperate situation of farmers in eastern
Adjournment Debate
Ontario, particularly farmers in parts of Dundas, Carleton and Grenville counties and indeed in other areas as well. The minister indicated that he had discussed the matter with the Ontario minister of agriculture and food and that his officials are carrying on the discussions.
This is not a satisfactory answer to the farmer who is caught in a dreadful position, not for the first time but for the second disastrous year in a row.
The farmer in eastern Ontario in 1972 is caught between the hammer and the anvil. First, it is the second year of disaster. Last year through wetness he could not take off the crop he planted, and this year he cannot get on his land to plant his crop. Never have I had as many anguished telephone calls from farmers as I have this year.
Secondly, farm input costs are galloping as never before. Statistics Canada has reported that farm input prices went up 6.1 per cent in the first quarter of 1973, a total increase of 10.2 per cent since the first quarter of 1972. This increase is fed by the cost of livestock feed, seed, labour, replacement costs, fertilizer, credit, all of the things vital to farmers. These are the costs of production that would be regulated by my party's policy of economic controls.
How critical the situation is can be shown by the figures given to me by a farmer constituent a few days ago. Oats in May of 1972 were $42.95 per ton; in June of 1973 they were $83.95 a ton. Barley in May of 1972 was $46.75 per ton; in June of 1973 it was $86.65. And so it goes. These prices are at Prescott, Ontario, with the federal subsidy of $6 per ton included.
Thirdly, the eastern Ontario farmer finds himself undermined by the weather. I cannot blame the government for the rain and the wet weather, but I am prepared to blame them if, in the face of a steadily worsening situation, they only consult and do not act. I do not accept the assertion that it is too early to take action. For many farmers it is in fact too late. I ask the federal government to take the lead in bringing a measure of relief to the eastern Ontario farmer.
On the long term basis there ought to be a full investigation under the Inquiries Act into farm production costs. On the short run basis I would like the process of federal-provincial consultation to be speeded up to arrive at a conclusion. I would also like the Ontario Federation of Agriculture and other farm organizations directly involved to be included as formal parties.
I would like the federal government to remember that there are few, if any, farmers who have any surplus of hay or silage. The barns of eastern Ontario are empty. I have never seen dairymen so unsure of themselves. I have never seen more auction sales of farms and herds that are now gone from production, many of them forever. I ask the minister to look at the pages of the weekly newspapers and see the auction sales ads.
I do not believe I have to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the time for talk has come and gone; the time for leadership is now upon us. This has become a matter of public concern. The united counties of Stormont, Dundas and

July 3, 1973
Adjournment Debate
Glengarry have called on us. in no uncertain terms, for leadership. The Dundas County Federation of Agriculture has called for the same action. If these farms are to be saved, if there is to be a real effort to maintain them for supplying food in the future, I would like to see the following steps taken:
(1)	The counties of Dundas, Grenville and Carleton to be declared a disaster area.
(2)	That there be an assessment of the actual crop loss to farmers by the Crop Insurance Commission.
(3)	That the federal government take the lead with the Ontario government in suggesting an equal contribution by each of them to a forgiveable loan fund, to be provided to farmers on the basis of (a) an amount equal to at least two-thirds of the farmer's loss and (b) this loan to be forgiveable over a period of five years, with a provision for charging the loan, or the balance from time to time, against the farm over a period of five years, with the balance collectible if the farm is sold within the five year period; otherwise it ought to be forgiven at 20 per cent per year over the five year period.
If the answer is to be that this would be an expensive proposition, I ask the government to consider the expense to consumers as a result of the disaster in eastern Ontario, and in other parts of Ontario, and to stack that cost against the cost of the program itself. This is an industry in peril, and the situation requires dramatic action by the whole community. I hope we will have evidence from the Minister of Agriculture tonight of what dramatic action the government proposes.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-EASTERN ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR AID TO FARMERS BECAUSE WET CONDITIONS PROHIBIT PLANTING OF CROPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question that the hon. member raises is one of great concern to me and my officials, and to many people in different parts of Canada, because this is not the only part of Canada that had trouble this year from wet weather conditions. This is true with respect to the Peace River district in both Alberta and British Columbia. It is true of parts of northern Saskatchewan, where some 70 townships are affected by wet conditions. It is not an isolated condition in eastern Ontario; it also exists in great parts of the province of Quebec where farmers have not been able to sow crops.
As I mentioned to the hon. member earlier, I have discussed this situation with the Minister of Agriculture
for Ontario. Also his officials, and other officials from the province have had discussions with my department concerning this situation. However, I remind the hon. member that the principal responsibility for developing proposals for assistance rests with the provincial government or provincial governments concerned. The policy has been that the federal government will assist, upon request by the province or provinces concerned, with the cost of assistance programs where these programs would impose a financial hardship on the province or provinces.
The government's main program to assist farmers when crops are below normal is of course the crop insurance program, which is administered jointly with the provinces. I am sure all hon. members are aware of the very positive amendments which have been proposed to make crop insurance an even better buy. I have been telling farmers that crop insurance is a good investment, and I note that farmers across Canada have increased their participation in crop insurance by 100 per cent over last year. In eastern Canada, as anywhere else in Canada, those farmers with crop insurance have income protection.
The hon. member seems to have made a study of farm costs. I congratulate him on this. I hope he passes his information on to some of his colleagues who seem to think that farmers can produce food cheaply despite the high input costs to which they are subjected. Very little can be done about some of these costs when the products used, as in the case of protein, are imported. A disaster must be declared first and foremost by the prophets.
In the case of farmers in certain counties in eastern Ontario, special provisions have been made under the federal-provincial crop insurance agreement to extend the date for seeding to enable farmers to get a crop in and still qualify for crop insurance. Second, we have amended our agreement with the Ontario crop insurance commission to extend insurance coverage for corn, spring grain, soya beans and white and coloured beans even if farmers holding crop insurance contracts are not able to get a crop planted.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I am aware of this situation and can assure the hon. member that if the federal government is approached by any province with disastrous crop conditions, this request will be given every consideration.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.27 p.m.
